q: When the inscription was discovered upon the wall I was more inclined than ever to my opinion. The thing was too evidently a blind.

s: the cab is driven by Jefferson Hope (during the murder of Enoch Drebber)
q: I had already determined in my own mind that the man who had walked into the house with Drebber, was none other than the man who had driven the cab.

s: the cab is a growler (identified by the narrow gauge of its wheels)
q: I satisfied myself that it was a cab and not a private carriage by the narrow gauge of the wheels. The ordinary London growler is considerably less wide than a gentleman’s brougham.

s: the newspaper report about the case credits Inspector Gregson (and Inspector Lestrade with the capture)
q: It is an open secret that the credit of this smart capture belongs entirely to the well-known Scotland Yard officials, Messrs. Lestrade and Gregson.

s: the newspaper report about the case attributes the romantic feud (as the cause of the crimes, involving love and Mormonism)
q: The details of the case will probably be never known now, though we are informed upon good authority that the crime was the result of an old standing and romantic feud, in which love and Mormonism bore a part.

s: the romantic feud involves Mormonism (according to the newspaper report)
q: The details of the case will probably be never known now, though we are informed upon good authority that the crime was the result of an old standing and romantic feud, in which love and Mormonism bore a part.

s: Enoch Drebber belongs to Mormons (in his younger days)
q: It seems that both the victims belonged, in their younger days, to the Latter Day Saints

s: Joseph Stangerson belongs to Mormons (in his younger days)
q: It seems that both the victims belonged, in their younger days, to the Latter Day Saints

s: Jefferson Hope is in Europe (at the time of the investigation)
q: The answer was conclusive. It told me that Drebber had already applied for the protection of the law against an old rival in love, named Jefferson Hope, and that this same Hope was at present in Europe.

s: Jefferson Hope is subject to the romantic feud (as an old rival in love of Enoch Drebber)
q: It told me that Drebber had already applied for the protection of the law against an old rival in love, named Jefferson Hope

s: the testimonial is intended for Inspector Gregson (and Inspector Lestrade, as public recognition of their supposed services)
q: It is expected that a testimonial of some sort will be presented to the two officers as a fitting recognition of their services.

s: Jefferson Hope hails from Salt Lake City
q: It seems that both the victims belonged, in their younger days, to the Latter Day Saints, and Hope, the deceased prisoner, hails also from Salt Lake City.

s: Sherlock Holmes is a detective (an amateur according to the newspaper report)
q: The man was apprehended, it appears, in the rooms of a certain Mr. Sherlock Holmes, who has himself, as an amateur, shown some talent in the detective line

s: Sherlock Holmes solves the Drebber–Stangerson murder investigation (within three days using ordinary deductions)
q: The proof of its intrinsic simplicity is, that without any help save a few very ordinary deductions I was able to lay my hand upon the criminal within three days.

s: Doctor Watson is a doctor of medicine
q: In the year 1878 I took my degree of Doctor of Medicine of the University of London

s: Doctor Watson resides at private hotel (in the Strand)
q: There I stayed for some time at a private hotel in the Strand

s: Doctor Watson has habits gets up at ungodly hours (during his current convalescence)
q: I get up at all sorts of ungodly hours, and I am extremely lazy.

s: Doctor Watson is lazy extremely (by his own account)
q: I get up at all sorts of ungodly hours, and I am extremely lazy.

s: Doctor Watson keeps bull pup
q: I keep a bull pup

s: Doctor Watson objects to rows (because his nerves are shaken)
q: I object to rows because my nerves are shaken

s: Doctor Watson knows young Stamford (as a former dresser under him at Barts)
q: young Stamford, who had been a dresser under me at Barts.

s: Doctor Watson prefers having a partner (to being alone)
q: I should prefer having a partner to being alone.

s: Doctor Watson has been in Afghanistan (during military service)
q: You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.

s: Doctor Watson serves as Assistant Surgeon (with the Fifth Northumberland Fusiliers)
q: I was duly attached to the Fifth Northumberland Fusiliers as Assistant Surgeon.

s: Sherlock Holmes is well versed in anatomy (according to young Stamford)
q: I believe he is well up in anatomy, and he is a first-class chemist

s: Sherlock Holmes takes medical studies (no systematic classes)
q: as far as I know, he has never taken out any systematic medical classes.

s: Sherlock Holmes possesses out-of-the-way knowledge (amassed through desultory and eccentric studies)
q: His studies are very desultory and eccentric, but he has amassed a lot of out-of-the-way knowledge which would astonish his professors.

s: Sherlock Holmes has temperament cold-blooded (in his scientific manner)
q: Holmes is a little too scientific for my tastes—it approaches to cold-bloodedness.

s: Sherlock Holmes seeks definite and exact knowledge (as a passion)
q: He appears to have a passion for definite and exact knowledge.

s: Sherlock Holmes beats the subjects (in the dissecting-rooms with a stick)
q: When it comes to beating the subjects in the dissecting-rooms with a stick, it is certainly taking rather a bizarre shape.

s: Sherlock Holmes could give a friend a little pinch of the latest vegetable alkaloid (out of a spirit of inquiry)
q: I could imagine his giving a friend a little pinch of the latest vegetable alkaloid, not out of malevolence, you understand, but simply out of a spirit of inquiry in order to have an accurate idea of the effects.

s: Sherlock Holmes works at chemical laboratory (intermittently, sometimes from morning to night)
q: He either avoids the place for weeks, or else he works there from morning to night.

s: Sherlock Holmes discovers Sherlock Holmes’ test (a medico-legal test for blood stains)
q: Now we have the Sherlock Holmes’ test, and there will no longer be any difficulty

s: Sherlock Holmes uses hæmoglobin (as the basis of his blood test)
q: I have found a re-agent which is precipitated by hæmoglobin, and by nothing else.

s: Doctor Watson serves with Berkshires (during the Afghan campaign)
q: I was removed from my brigade and attached to the Berkshires, with whom I served at the fatal battle of Maiwand.

s: Sherlock Holmes dabbles in poisons (frequently)
q: I have to be careful,” he continued, turning to me with a smile, “for I dabble with poisons a good deal.

s: Sherlock Holmes smokes strong tobacco (habitually enough to warn a prospective lodger)
q: You don’t mind the smell of strong tobacco, I hope?

s: Sherlock Holmes asks about violin-playing
q: Do you include violin-playing in your category of rows?” he asked, anxiously.

s: Sherlock Holmes seeks to share suite of rooms (with Dr. Watson at Baker Street)
q: I have my eye on a suite in Baker Street,” he said, “which would suit us down to the ground.

s: Sherlock Holmes has moods dumps (sometimes, with periods of silence)
q: I get in the dumps at times, and don’t open my mouth for days on end.

s: Sherlock Holmes has eye on a suite in Baker Street (which would suit us down to the ground)
q: I have my eye on a suite in Baker Street,” he said, “which would suit us down to the ground.

s: young Stamford is a dresser (formerly under Dr. Watson at Barts)
q: young Stamford, who had been a dresser under me at Barts.

s: young Stamford knows Sherlock Holmes (through occasional meetings in the laboratory)
q: I know nothing more of him than I have learned from meeting him occasionally in the laboratory.

s: young Stamford introduces Doctor Watson (to Sherlock Holmes as a prospective lodger)
q: Dr. Watson, Mr. Sherlock Holmes,” said Stamford, introducing us.

s: Doctor Watson is wounded by Jezail bullet (in the shoulder at the battle of Maiwand)
q: There I was struck on the shoulder by a Jezail bullet, which shattered the bone and grazed the subclavian artery.

s: University of London awards degree to Doctor Watson (Doctor of Medicine)
q: I took my degree of Doctor of Medicine of the University of London

s: Fifth Northumberland Fusiliers has member Doctor Watson (as Assistant Surgeon)
q: I was duly attached to the Fifth Northumberland Fusiliers as Assistant Surgeon.

s: hæmoglobin reacts with Sherlock Holmes’ test (the reagent is precipitated by it)
q: I have found a re-agent which is precipitated by hæmoglobin, and by nothing else.

s: Sherlock Holmes’ test is more reliable than Guiacum test (according to Sherlock Holmes)
q: Beautiful! beautiful! The old Guiacum test was very clumsy and uncertain.

s: Sherlock Holmes’ test is more reliable than microscopic examination for blood corpuscles (especially for old stains)
q: So is the microscopic examination for blood corpuscles. The latter is valueless if the stains are a few hours old.

s: blood stains are detectable by Sherlock Holmes’ test (even when old)
q: Now, this appears to act as well whether the blood is old or new.

s: Doctor Watson meets Sherlock Holmes (at the chemical laboratory through young Stamford)
q: “Dr. Watson, Mr. Sherlock Holmes,” said Stamford, introducing us.

s: Doctor Watson is rescued from Ghazis (by Murray)
q: I should have fallen into the hands of the murderous Ghazis had it not been for the devotion and courage shown by Murray, my orderly, who threw me across a pack-horse, and succeeded in bringing me safely to the British lines.

s: Doctor Watson contracts enteric fever (while recovering at Peshawar)
q: when I was struck down by enteric fever, that curse of our Indian possessions.

s: Doctor Watson has health irretrievably ruined (after the Afghan campaign and enteric fever)
q: landed a month later on Portsmouth jetty, with my health irretrievably ruined

s: Doctor Watson receives income eleven shillings and sixpence a day (from the government)
q: was therefore as free as air—or as free as an income of eleven shillings and sixpence a day will permit a man to be

s: Doctor Watson has no relatives in England (no kith or kin)
q: I had neither kith nor kin in England

s: Sherlock Holmes inspects the rooms at No. 221B, Baker Street
q: We met next day as he had arranged, and inspected the rooms at No. 221B, Baker Street, of which he had spoken at our meeting.

s: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities includes geology (practical but limited)
q: 6. Geology.—Practical, but limited. Tells at a glance different soils from each other.

s: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities includes sensational literature (immense)
q: 9. Sensational Literature.—Immense. He appears to know every detail of every horror perpetrated in the century.

s: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities includes the violin (plays it well)
q: 10. Plays the violin well.

s: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities includes British law (good practical knowledge)
q: 12. Has a good practical knowledge of British law.

s: Sherlock Holmes has knowledge of crime and criminals (through study of the history of crime)
q: They lay all the evidence before me, and I am generally able, by the help of my knowledge of the history of crime, to set them straight.

s: Sherlock Holmes serves Government detectives (when they are at fault)
q: Here in London we have lots of Government detectives and lots of private ones. When these fellows are at fault they come to me, and I manage to put them on the right scent.

s: Sherlock Holmes serves private inquiry agencies (through people sent on to him)
q: They are mostly sent on by private inquiry agencies.

s: Sherlock Holmes has clients Holmes's clients (people in trouble seeking enlightenment)
q: I have to use this room as a place of business,” he said, “and these people are my clients.”

s: Sherlock Holmes has special knowledge (applied to investigative problems)
q: You see I have a lot of special knowledge which I apply to the problem, and which facilitates matters wonderfully.

s: Sherlock Holmes deduces origin of Afghanistan (from Dr. Watson's appearance and condition)
q: Clearly in Afghanistan.’ The whole train of thought did not occupy a second. I then remarked that you came from Afghanistan, and you were astonished.”

s: Doctor Watson moves things from the hotel (that very evening)
q: That very evening I moved my things round from the hotel, and on the following morning Sherlock Holmes followed me with several boxes and portmanteaus.

s: Sherlock Holmes knows Lestrade (a well-known detective who consulted him)
q: Lestrade is a well-known detective. He got himself into a fog recently over a forgery case, and that was what brought him here.”

s: Sherlock Holmes criticizes C. Auguste Dupin (considers him inferior and superficial)
q: No doubt you think that you are complimenting me in comparing me to Dupin,” he observed. “Now, in my opinion, Dupin was a very inferior fellow.

s: Sherlock Holmes criticizes Monsieur Lecoq (considers him a miserable bungler)
q: Lecoq was a miserable bungler,” he said, in an angry voice; “he had only one thing to recommend him, and that was his energy.

s: Sherlock Holmes plays the violin (remarkably and eccentrically)
q: I see that I have alluded above to his powers upon the violin. These were very remarkable, but as eccentric as all his other accomplishments.

s: Doctor Watson is a army doctor (recently returned from Afghanistan)
q: Here is a gentleman of a medical type, but with the air of a military man. Clearly an army doctor, then.

s: Doctor Watson comes from Afghanistan (as inferred by Sherlock Holmes)
q: I then remarked that you came from Afghanistan, and you were astonished.”

s: the retired sergeant of Marines is a Royal Marine Light Infantry (formerly a sergeant)
q: “A sergeant, sir, Royal Marine Light Infantry, sir. No answer? Right, sir.”

s: the retired sergeant of Marines is a commissionaire (currently serving in civilian employment)
q: “May I ask, my lad,” I said, in the blandest voice, “what your trade may be?” “Commissionaire, sir,” he said, gruffly. “Uniform away for repairs.”

s: Sherlock Holmes is a consulting detective work (his own trade)
q: Well, I have a trade of my own. I suppose I am the only one in the world. I’m a consulting detective, if you can understand what that is.

s: London contains Government detectives (in considerable numbers)
q: Here in London we have lots of Government detectives and lots of private ones.

s: London has lots of private ones (here in London)
q: Here in London we have lots of Government detectives and lots of private ones.

s: Sherlock Holmes practises observation and deduction (as the basis of his professional work)
q: Yes, I have a turn both for observation and for deduction. The theories which I have expressed there, and which appear to you to be so chimerical are really extremely practical—so practical that I depend upon them for my bread and cheese.

s: the Science of Deduction and Analysis is a science (acquired through long and patient study)
q: Like all other arts, the Science of Deduction and Analysis is one which can only be acquired by long and patient study nor, is life long enough to allow any mortal to attain the highest possible perfection in it.

s: The Book of Life is a article (about observation and deduction)
q: Its somewhat ambitious title was “The Book of Life,” and it attempted to show how much an observant man might learn by an accurate and systematic examination of all that came in his way.

s: The Book of Life is written by Sherlock Holmes
q: “As for the article, I wrote it myself.”

s: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities includes chemistry (profound)
q: 7. Chemistry.—Profound.

s: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities includes anatomy (accurate but unsystematic)
q: 8. Anatomy.—Accurate, but unsystematic.

s: Sherlock Holmes is an unofficial personage
q: That comes of being an unofficial personage.

s: Enoch Drebber is a deceased gentleman (found in 3, Lauriston Gardens)
q: He found the door open, and in the front room, which is bare of furniture, discovered the body of a gentleman, well dressed, and having cards in his pocket bearing the name of ‘Enoch J. Drebber, Cleveland, Ohio, U.S.A.’

s: Enoch Drebber has residence or origin Cleveland, Ohio (identified by cards in his pocket)
q: having cards in his pocket bearing the name of ‘Enoch J. Drebber, Cleveland, Ohio, U.S.A.’

s: Enoch Drebber is about to return to New York (by ship from Liverpool)
q: It is clear that this unfortunate man was about to return to New York.

s: Enoch Drebber possesses the gold watch (found in his pockets)
q: A gold watch, No. 97163, by Barraud, of London.
